Low EMF means roughly 5–10 mG, ultra-low 3–5 mG and near-zero 2–3 mG. Those are manufacturer conventions rather than a standard, and the reading depends entirely on the distance it was taken at — which most listings do not state. If you're shopping for an infrared sauna, you've probably run into phrases like "low EMF," "ultra-low EMF," and "near-zero EMF" — often stamped on nearly identical cabins carrying very different price tags. It's easy to assume the lower number is the safer, healthier choice and that paying more is simply the responsible thing to do.

Here's the honest version: none of those phrases is a regulated category. They're manufacturer design targets, not safety standards. And most reputable home saunas already run far below the international exposure limits set for the general public. This guide explains what the labels actually mean, how to read an EMF spec without being misled, who genuinely benefits from paying extra, and exactly what to verify before you buy — without fear-based selling.

The short answer. For most healthy adults, a reputable low-EMF sauna is plenty — both low-EMF and near-zero-EMF cabins typically operate hundreds of times below the general-public reference level. Near-zero / ultra-low EMF is a reasonable precaution or peace-of-mind upgrade, not a proven health improvement. If money is tight, spend it on cabin size, heater coverage, and warranty first — and always confirm a published EMF number with its test distance, plus real electrical-safety certification, before you trust any label.

What "Low EMF," "Ultra-Low EMF," and "Near-Zero EMF" Actually Mean

No regulator — not the ICNIRP, the World Health Organization, or any U.S. agency — defines a "low EMF sauna" or a "near-zero EMF sauna," and none sets a milligauss cutoff for those words. They're voluntary marketing and engineering labels chosen by manufacturers.

One more clarification that trips up almost every buyer: in sauna listings, "EMF" almost always means the 50/60 Hz alternating magnetic field produced by electricity flowing through the wiring and heating elements. It does not mean the infrared heat itself (that's a separate, non-ionizing thermal energy), and it isn't the same as radiofrequency EMF from phones or Wi-Fi. Keeping those straight is the whole game.

How the industry uses the three tiers

These ranges are common industry practice — useful shorthand, but remember they're marketing conventions, not regulated bands, and they're usually measured close to a panel:

Tier (marketing label) Typical published reading What it really signals
Standard (not marketed as low-EMF) ~20–100+ mG near heaters No special EMF engineering; still usually well under safety limits
Low EMF ~5–10 mG at ~2–3" from a panel Panels wired to reduce the magnetic field; the mainstream choice
Ultra-Low EMF Usually "under 3 mG" A lower design target; often a small price step above low-EMF
Near-Zero EMF Claimed low single digits / near background The most aggressive target; frequently paired with full-spectrum heaters

InHouse Wellness organizes its infrared cabins into three of these buckets you can browse directly — Low EMF, Ultra-Low EMF, and Near-Zero EMF. (Ultra-low inventory rotates; check availability on the collection or individual product pages.)

Why Test Distance and Method Matter More Than the Number

A magnetic field falls off steeply as you move away from its source. That single fact is why raw milligauss numbers are so easy to misread.

Picture the same sauna measured two ways: a reading taken with the meter pressed a couple of inches from a heating panel will be far higher than one taken at your seated torso a foot away. Both numbers can be completely honest — and completely different. So a "5–10 mG at 2–3 inches" spec and an "under 3 mG" spec with no distance listed aren't really comparable; the second one might simply have been measured farther away.

The rule that protects you: only compare EMF numbers measured the same way — same distance, same location in the cabin, same operating state (heaters actively cycling produce the highest readings). If a listing gives a milligauss figure but no test distance, treat the number as incomplete and ask for the distance before you weigh it.

Are These EMF Levels Considered Safe?

When a sauna is properly built and electrically certified, both low-EMF and near-zero-EMF cabins operate far below the exposure guidance set for the general public.

The reference point is the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP). In its 2010 low-frequency guidelines, the general-public reference level for 50/60 Hz magnetic fields is 200 microtesla — which equals 2,000 milligauss. Put that next to a quality home sauna:

Reading Compared to the 2,000 mG public reference level
Standard sauna, ~20–100 mG Roughly 20–100× below the reference level
Low-EMF sauna, ~5–10 mG Roughly 200–400× below
Near-zero / ultra-low, under 3 mG Over 600× below

A fair caveat: those sauna readings are usually taken a few inches from a panel, while the reference level describes whole-body exposure — so treat the ratios as order-of-magnitude, not exact. Either way, the margin is large.


Two things "below the limit" does not mean. It doesn't mean "zero risk," and it doesn't mean "healthier." A reference level marks the threshold below which known effects aren't expected — it's a screening tool, not a product-quality score. A lower milligauss number doesn't buy you a documented health benefit.

What the cancer research actually says

This is where careful wording matters. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies extremely-low-frequency magnetic fields as Group 2B, "possibly carcinogenic to humans." That classification rests mainly on epidemiological studies linking childhood leukaemia to higher residential exposure — specifically a time-weighted 24-hour average above about 0.3–0.4 µT (3–4 mG). Importantly, animal and laboratory evidence hasn't established that these fields cause leukaemia, and IARC placed ELF electric fields in Group 3 ("not classifiable"), with no evidence of a link to other cancers.

Why does that not translate into a sauna alarm? Because the 3–4 mG figure is a round-the-clock home average, not a brief reading taken inches from a panel during a 30-minute session. The two aren't the same measurement, and it would be misleading to line them up as if a low-EMF sauna "exceeds a cancer threshold." The WHO's assessment is consistent with this: established biological effects appear only at much higher field strengths (well above 100 µT), and long-term, low-level exposure evidence remains mixed and inconclusive.

Infrared itself is worth one clear sentence: it's non-ionizing thermal energy — fundamentally different from ionizing radiation like X-rays. An infrared sauna does not emit ionizing radiation.

Magnetic Field vs Electric Field: The Detail Most Listings Skip

"EMF" bundles together two different things, and a sauna can score well on one while saying nothing about the other:

  • The AC magnetic field (measured in milligauss or microtesla) comes from current flowing through the heaters and wiring. This is the number almost every sauna page advertises.
  • The AC electric field (measured in volts per meter) comes from voltage on the wiring. Reducing the magnetic field doesn't automatically reduce the electric field — they're addressed by different design choices like grounding, shielding, and wire routing.

In practice, sauna sellers — InHouse Wellness included — typically publish a magnetic-field figure and don't list electric-field data. That's normal for the category, but it means a single "low EMF" number is a partial picture. It's reasonable to ask a brand whether the electric field was measured and mitigated; just don't expect every listing to have that answer, and don't treat the absence as a red flag on its own.

Low EMF vs Near-Zero EMF: Side-by-Side

Factor Standard Low EMF Ultra-Low / Near-Zero
Typical magnetic reading ~20–100+ mG near heaters ~5–10 mG at 2–3" Usually under 3 mG (distance often unstated)
Electric-field data Rarely published Rarely published Occasionally emphasized; still often absent
Margin vs public limit ~20–100× below ~200–400× below 600×+ below
Typical cost Lowest Mid-range Premium (often a modest step up)
Best for Budget buyers who still want certification Most buyers — balance of value, features, safety margin EMF-cautious buyers wanting maximum reassurance

The one comparison that teaches the whole lesson

Look closely at the two San Marino cabins. They share a footprint and a six-panel layout — the only real difference is the EMF label and how each reports its number. The standard San Marino ($2,299) publishes "5–10 mG at 2–3 inches" — a reading and its distance. The Elite ($2,499) advertises a lower "under 3 mG" but doesn't state the distance, so you can't actually conclude it's two-to-three times quieter; the figure may simply have been taken farther from the panel. Both are legitimate cabins. The standard is the better-documented value; the Elite is the pick if the lowest advertised tier gives you peace of mind and you want the model with the most reviews. Either way, the takeaway is the same: trust the listing that shows its methodology.

Who Should Actually Pay Extra for Near-Zero EMF?

Near-zero EMF isn't necessary for most people. It's a preference-driven upgrade that makes sense for specific buyers. You may reasonably choose it if you:

  • Report EMF sensitivity or simply feel more at ease with the lowest advertised number (worth noting: the WHO recognizes that symptoms people attribute to EMF are real for them, but a causal link to field exposure hasn't been established).
  • Are already buying a premium, full-spectrum cabin and view ultra-low EMF as part of the package.
  • Value maximum precaution for its own sake and have room in the budget.

A reputable low-EMF cabin is the better call if you're an everyday value buyer, you'd rather put dollars toward a bigger cabin, better heater coverage, or a longer warranty, or you're comfortable relying on established safety margins. There's no evidence that daily use or longer sessions creates a threshold where near-zero suddenly becomes necessary, and no study shows that dropping a cabin from roughly 8 mG to 2 mG delivers a measurable health benefit.

Children, pregnancy, pacemakers, and medical devices: these are heat-and-medical-device questions, not EMF-tier questions. Public exposure limits are set with safety margins intended to cover children and adults alike — but if any of these apply to you, the right move is to talk with your healthcare provider before using any infrared sauna, regardless of its EMF label.

A Simple Decision Framework

Instead of chasing the lowest number, judge the quality of the claim and how much EMF actually matters to you. Work down this list:

  1. Does the listing publish an actual magnetic-field number? No number → ask before buying.
  2. Is the test distance stated? No distance → treat the number as incomplete.
  3. Is the operating condition/location described? (Which panel, heaters running?)
  4. Is electric-field data available? Usually no across the category — that's normal, but nice to have.
  5. Can you verify the electrical-safety listing (UL/ETL/CSA) for that exact model?
  6. Is reducing EMF a genuine personal priority for you? If yes, near-zero is a fair choice.
  7. Would the price gap be better spent on size, heaters, warranty, or comfort? Very often, yes.

Three outcomes fall out of that: a well-documented low-EMF cabin (best value for most), an ultra-low / near-zero cabin (peace of mind), or walk away if there's no published data and no verifiable certification.

What to Verify Before You Buy

Verify this Why it matters How to check
Published magnetic-field reading and test distance A number without a distance can't be compared fairly Look on the spec sheet for "mG at X inches"; ask if it's missing
Electric-field status Low magnetic doesn't guarantee low electric field Ask whether EF was measured; accept that many brands don't publish it
UL / ETL / CSA listing for the complete sauna Protects against shock and fire — the real safety risks Confirm the model in the Intertek or UL database, not just a logo on the page
Heater type, count, and coverage Drives comfort and heat distribution far more than EMF tier Review the heater layout (walls, bench, floor) in the specs
Warranty terms Reflects real long-term value Check length and what's covered (structure, heaters, electronics)

Certification does not verify EMF. UL, ETL (Intertek), and CSA are electrical-safety marks — they test for shock, fire, and flammability, not for milligauss levels. A safety listing is essential, but it says nothing about a cabin's EMF performance, and vice-versa. Treat them as two separate checks.

Common Mistakes Buyers Make

  • Treating the labels as regulated. "Low," "ultra-low," and "near-zero" are marketing targets, not certified categories.
  • Comparing numbers measured at different distances. "Under 3 mG" with no distance can't be ranked against "5–10 mG at 2–3 inches."
  • Assuming a lower reading means a healthier sauna. At these levels, no health benefit has been demonstrated for going lower.
  • Thinking a UL/ETL logo verifies EMF. It verifies electrical safety only.
  • Buying on EMF alone. Build quality, heater coverage, cabin size, and warranty affect your experience far more.
  • Rewiring an existing cabin to "lower EMF." That's an electrician's job, can void warranties, and is usually not worth it versus a purpose-built unit.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the difference between low EMF and near-zero EMF?

Both are manufacturer labels, not regulated categories. Near-zero / ultra-low targets a lower advertised reading (often "under 3 mG") than low EMF (around 5–10 mG measured close to a panel). Neither is defined by a regulator.

Is near-zero EMF safer than low EMF?

There's no demonstrated health difference between them at these levels. Near-zero is best understood as a precaution or peace-of-mind choice rather than a safety upgrade.

What EMF level counts as "low" in an infrared sauna?

Industry practice puts "low EMF" around 5–10 mG measured a couple of inches from a panel — but that's a marketing convention, not an official cutoff.

What does "under 3 mG" mean, and can I trust it?

It's a magnetic-field reading below 3 milligauss. It's only meaningful with a stated test distance and operating condition, which listings often omit. Ask for the distance before you compare it to another cabin's number.

At what distance should sauna EMF be measured?

There's no universal standard. Brands report anywhere from the panel surface to your seated position, so a reading only means something alongside its distance. Compare like with like.

Is EMF the same as the electric field?

No. The magnetic field (milligauss) and the electric field (volts per meter) are separate. Reducing one doesn't automatically reduce the other, and most sauna listings only publish the magnetic figure.

Do infrared saunas emit radiation?

They emit non-ionizing infrared (heat) plus small low-frequency magnetic fields from the wiring. That's completely different from ionizing radiation such as X-rays.

Does UL or ETL certification verify EMF performance?

No. Those marks confirm electrical safety (shock, fire, flammability). EMF performance is a separate measurement.

Is near-zero EMF worth the extra cost?

It depends on your priorities. There's no measured health benefit over a certified low-EMF cabin at these levels, so it comes down to how much peace of mind the lower number gives you versus spending that money on size, heaters, or warranty.

Does a lower EMF reading guarantee better health outcomes?

No. A lower number does not translate into a documented health benefit.

Bottom Line: Which Should You Choose?

Both low-EMF and near-zero-EMF infrared saunas are generally safe when properly certified, and both sit far below the general-public exposure reference level. The real difference is precautionary design and personal values — not medical necessity.

  • For most buyers: a certified low-EMF cabin (around 5–10 mG) is sufficient and the best value.
  • For EMF-cautious buyers: ultra-low / near-zero offers extra reassurance and often costs only modestly more.
  • For everyone: prioritize a transparent EMF number with its distance, verifiable UL/ETL/CSA certification, solid heater coverage, and a real warranty over the label on the box.

What We Still Don't Know

The science here is reassuring but not finished. Health agencies acknowledge that evidence on long-term, low-level exposure to low-frequency magnetic fields remains mixed, which is exactly why some buyers prefer precautionary ultra-low designs. There's no consensus on whether the symptoms some people attribute to EMF are physiological, and no large study has compared long-term health outcomes between low-EMF and near-zero-EMF sauna users. These are open questions, not warning signs — guidelines are updated as evidence develops, and at today's exposure levels both tiers represent conservative choices.
